title: Inspect working donkeys living and working under sub-optimal welfare conditions

lessons.title: Donkey physiology and how it differs from the horse
lessons.html:
A different animal, not a small horse

Welfare inspectors often assess donkeys as if they were small horses. This leads to wrong conclusions. The donkey evolved in semi-arid, rocky country in north-east Africa, and its body and behaviour reflect that origin. Understanding the differences is the foundation of a fair, accurate inspection.

Key physiological differences

FeatureDonkeyPractical meaning for the inspector
Water balanceTolerates considerable dehydration and can drink large volumes quickly to recoverA donkey may not show obvious thirst; check water access rather than relying on behaviour
DigestionVery efficient on fibrous, low-quality forageRich feeds and lush pasture lead to obesity and laminitis
Fat storageStores fat in the neck crest, rump and flanksBody condition must be scored on donkey-specific criteria; a fat crest can remain when the animal is thin elsewhere
Metabolic riskProne to hyperlipaemia when it stops eatingAny donkey off its feed is a veterinary emergency
CoatLess waterproof than a horse's coatNeeds shelter from rain and cold wind
HoovesMore upright, adapted to dry, hard ground; absorb moistureWet, muddy conditions cause hoof disease
BehaviourStoic: shows pain and illness very littleSubtle signs such as dullness or standing apart can indicate serious disease

Other differences

  • Larger ears and a different voice (the bray).
  • Normal temperature, pulse and breathing ranges differ from the horse; use donkey-specific reference ranges supplied by your vet or welfare organisation rather than horse values.
  • Drug doses and responses differ from horses; treatment decisions belong to a veterinarian.
  • Mules and hinnies (donkey-horse crosses) share some traits of each parent and should be assessed with this in mind.

Implication for inspection

Inspectors must avoid two errors: over-reacting to normal donkey features (a calm, still animal that is simply conserving energy) and under-reacting to quiet signs of real suffering. A donkey that stands with its head low, does not respond to its surroundings and will not eat may be seriously ill even if it is not distressed in an obvious way.

lessons.title: Health parameters, common ailments and handling
lessons.html:
Recognising a healthy donkey

  • Alert, interested in surroundings, ears mobile
  • Eating and drinking; passing normal firm droppings and urine
  • Clear eyes and nostrils without discharge
  • Even weight bearing on all four feet, sound at walk
  • Coat and skin intact, without wounds or heavy parasite burden
  • Body condition neither emaciated nor obese, scored on a donkey-specific scale

Record temperature, pulse and respiration against the donkey reference ranges your organisation uses, and record the capillary refill and gut sounds where you are trained to do so.

Common problems in working donkeys

ProblemTypical cause
Harness and saddle woundsPoor, unpadded or wire harness; overloading
Overgrown or diseased hoovesNo trimming; wet, dirty standing areas
LamenessHoof neglect, overwork on hard roads, injury
Dental diseaseUneven wear, age; leads to weight loss
Poor body conditionUnderfeeding, parasites, teeth, overwork
Internal and external parasitesNo deworming or tick control
Wounds from beating, hobbles or tethersInhumane handling and restraint
Hyperlipaemia, colic, respiratory diseaseStress, starvation, poor feeding

Humane handling

Donkeys are intelligent and cautious. When frightened they tend to freeze and plant their feet rather than flee, which is often misread as stubbornness. Force and beating make this worse and are illegal cruelty.

  • Approach calmly from the side towards the shoulder, speaking quietly.
  • Allow the donkey to smell your hand; scratch the withers.
  • Use a correctly fitted halter, not a wire or thin rope around the nose or jaw.
  • To move a reluctant donkey, give it time, lead from beside the shoulder, and use a companion donkey to lead the way.
  • Never twist ears, tie legs tightly, or use sticks with nails.

Behavioural problems

Kicking, biting, refusal to move and head-shyness are usually learned responses to pain, fear or rough handling. The inspector should look for the cause: a sore mouth from a bit, wounds under the harness, or a history of beating. Correcting the cause and handling gently are the solutions. Donkeys are herd animals and can become distressed when kept alone; stallions may be aggressive and need experienced handling.

lessons.title: Harness, equipment and work
lessons.html:
Equipment on a traction donkey

In South Africa donkeys pull carts carrying water, firewood, building materials and people, and some still plough. Correct equipment spreads the load safely; poor equipment is the single biggest cause of wounds in working donkeys.

ItemFunctionWelfare concerns
Collar or breastbandTransfers pulling force from the chest and shouldersRubs and pressure sores if too tight, unpadded, or made of wire, tyre strips or thin rope
Saddle / back padSupports the shafts and spreads weightBack sores if unpadded or poorly placed; pressure on the spine
Girth / belly bandHolds saddle and shafts in placeGirth galls from thin or dirty straps
TracesConnect collar or breastband to the cartUneven length pulls the animal crooked; chains can cut legs
BreechingLets the donkey hold back the cart when slowing or going downhillWithout it the cart pushes into the donkey; sores on hindquarters
Bridle and bitSteering and stoppingMouth wounds from wire bits, rusty bits or harsh use; many donkeys work well without a bit
CartCarries the loadUnbalanced loads, no brakes, broken shafts, overloading

Inspecting and maintaining equipment

  • Remove the harness and inspect the skin underneath for hair loss, swelling and wounds.
  • Check that contact surfaces are wide, smooth and padded with soft material (sacking, foam or old blanket covered with cloth).
  • Check the fit: the collar or breastband should sit on the muscle of the chest, not on the windpipe or point of the shoulder.
  • Check the cart: balanced load, working wheels and bearings, shafts at the correct height, brakes where possible.
  • Advise owners on simple, low-cost improvements: padding, replacing wire with webbing or leather, cleaning harness regularly.

Uses and welfare needs

For many rural households a donkey is a source of income and transport. The welfare approach is therefore to keep the donkey working well, not simply to stop it working. Welfare needs can be framed as the Five Freedoms:

  • Freedom from hunger and thirst - forage, water and rest stops during work
  • Freedom from discomfort - shelter from rain, sun and wind; a dry place to stand
  • Freedom from pain, injury and disease - well-fitted harness, hoof and dental care, deworming
  • Freedom to express normal behaviour - company of other donkeys, time to roll and graze
  • Freedom from fear and distress - humane handling, no beating

Work should match the animal's age, size and condition: no work for very young, old, lame, heavily pregnant or sick donkeys; reasonable loads; regular rest and water; no working in the hottest part of the day where it can be avoided.

lessons.title: Legislation and conducting the inspection
lessons.html:
Relevant legislation

  • Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 - the main animal cruelty law. It makes it an offence to cruelly treat an animal, including overloading, overdriving or working an animal that is unfit, confining it without adequate space, food or water, and failing to obtain veterinary help for an animal in need. Confirm exact wording with your organisation's legal guidance.
  • Societies for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act 169 of 1993 - governs SPCAs and their authorised inspectors.
  • Animal Diseases Act 35 of 1984 - controlled and notifiable diseases, movement controls.
  • Road traffic legislation and municipal by-laws - may regulate animal-drawn vehicles on public roads, such as lights and reflectors, and where carts may operate.

Inspectors must act only within the powers their organisation and the law give them, and work with the SPCA, state veterinary services or the police where legal action is required.

Conducting an inspection in sub-optimal conditions

Most owners do not intend cruelty; poverty, lack of knowledge and lack of access to services are common causes. An effective inspection combines firm welfare standards with respect and education.

  1. Prepare: identification, inspection forms, thermometer, torch, camera, basic first aid kit, halter and padding materials.
  2. Introduce yourself to the owner, explain the purpose and ask permission to examine the animal.
  3. Observe from a distance: demeanour, posture, gait, body condition, interaction with handler.
  4. Examine closely: vital signs, eyes, nose, mouth and teeth if trained, skin and coat, harness areas, legs and hooves.
  5. Inspect the equipment and cart and the living area: water, feed, shelter, footing.
  6. Record findings objectively with date, location, owner details, photographs and body condition score.
  7. Agree actions with the owner: immediate rest, padding, wound treatment by a vet, hoof trimming, deworming. Set a follow-up date.
  8. Escalate serious or repeated cruelty to the SPCA, state vet or police according to procedure.

Example

In a village outside Kuruman an inspector finds a donkey with a weeping wound on the chest from a wire breastband. The owner uses the donkey to carry water to sell. The inspector shows how to replace the wire with a padded webbing band, arranges veterinary treatment and advises two weeks' rest, and books a follow-up visit. The record notes the wound size and photographs.

Key points

  • Donkeys are stoic, desert-adapted and metabolically different from horses; use donkey-specific references.
  • A donkey that stops eating is an emergency because of hyperlipaemia risk.
  • Poor harness and overloading are the main causes of wounds in working donkeys.
  • Handle donkeys calmly; "stubbornness" is often fear or pain.
  • The Animals Protection Act 71 of 1962 is the main cruelty law; record findings objectively and escalate serious cases.
